title: API Design
description: Designing resilient, evolvable, and secure service contracts: RESTful modeling, versioning, cursor pagination, idempotency, rate limiting, gateways, and auth.

subtopics.title: REST API Design
subtopics.subtitle: Resource-oriented noun hierarchies, HTTP verb semantics, RFC 7807 error envelopes, filtering, and handling non-CRUD actions cleanly.
keyTakeaways: Model URLs around plural resource **nouns** (`/v1/orders/{id}/items`), never RPC verbs (`/v1/createNewOrder`), and let HTTP methods (`GET`, `POST`, `PATCH`, `DELETE`) express the action.
Standardize error responses across all microservices using a machine-parsable envelope (RFC 7807 Problem Details) with stable error codes, request trace IDs, and field-level validation details.

When a business action doesn't map cleanly to CRUD (e.g., transferring funds or cancelling an order), model the action as a **sub-resource noun** (`POST /v1/orders/{id}/cancellation` or `POST /v1/transfers`).

+-------------------------------------------------------------------------+

sections.heading: 1. Architectural Fundamentals & Core Mechanics
sections.body: Representational State Transfer (REST), defined by Roy Fielding, treats every domain concept as an addressable **Resource** manipulated through standard HTTP verbs. Good REST APIs are predictable: once an engineer learns how `/v1/users` works, they immediately know how `/v1/invoices` works. Keep URL nesting to at most 2 levels (`/v1/organizations/{orgId}/members`); if you need deeper access, allow querying the child resource directly by its globally unique prefixed ID (`/v1/members/mem_892a`).
bullets: **Core Architectural Principle**: Model URLs around plural resource **nouns** (`/v1/orders/{id}/items`), never RPC verbs (`/v1/createNewOrder`), and let HTTP methods (`GET`, `POST`, `PATCH`, `DELETE`) express the action.

**Problem Space & Invariants**: Standardize error responses across all microservices using a machine-parsable envelope (RFC 7807 Problem Details) with stable error codes, request trace IDs, and field-level validation details.
**System Boundary**: Operates across client network dispatch, gateway queuing, thread execution pools, and persistent storage I/O.

sections.heading: 2. Architectural Patterns & Implementation Topologies
sections.body: Distributed architectures apply specific implementation patterns and topologies for REST API Design:
bullets: **Pure RESTful Resource API**: Provides leverages native http caching, status codes, and cdn semantics; predictable uniform interface; zero custom client tooling required. Best suited for Public platform APIs, microservice domain boundaries, and standard CRUD/resource-oriented SaaS products.

**GraphQL / BFF Aggregation Layer**: Provides clients fetch exact fields across multiple resources in a single round-trip; eliminates mobile over-fetching. Best suited for Complex UI dashboards and mobile apps aggregating data from 10+ microservices via a Backend-for-Frontend (BFF).

Opaque Prefixed IDs (Stripe Pattern): Use prefixed K-sortable IDs like `ord_01HQ8.` or `usr_01HQ8.` instead of sequential integers (`1, 2, 3`) to prevent ID enumeration attacks and make logs self-describing.
`PUT` vs `PATCH`: `PUT` replaces the entire resource representation (missing fields are nulled), whereas `PATCH` applies a partial update to only the provided fields.
Bulk Operations: Avoid N+1 client round-trips by offering batch endpoints (`POST /v1/messages:batchDelete`) that return per-item status arrays (`207 Multi-Status`).

Consistent Timestamps & Money: Always use ISO-8601 UTC strings (`2026-03-15T14:30:00Z`) for time and integer smallest-currency units (`amount_cents: 1999` + `currency: 'USD'`) to avoid IEEE 754 floating-point bugs.

sections.heading: 3. Production Strengths: Where & How to Apply
sections.body: Production deployments apply REST API Design across targeted operational scenarios:
bullets: **Where to Use: High-Impact Scenarios**: Optimal for Public platform APIs, microservice domain boundaries, and standard CRUD/resource-oriented SaaS products, suited for environments requiring Leverages native HTTP caching, status codes, and CDN semantics; predictable uniform interface; zero custom client tooling required.

**Where to Use: High-Throughput Scenarios**: Recommended for Complex UI dashboards and mobile apps aggregating data from 10+ microservices via a Backend-for-Frontend (BFF), where Clients fetch exact fields across multiple resources in a single round-trip; eliminates mobile over-fetching.

**How to Use: Engineering Implementation**: When a `POST` or `DELETE` operation takes longer than ~500ms (e.g., provisioning a database cluster or exporting a 10GB archive), do not hold the HTTP connection open. Always establish explicit thresholds, measurement baselines, and automated monitoring.
**Architectural Leverage**: Provides predictable resource boundaries, bounds blast radius, and optimizes cost per transaction.

sections.heading: 4. Failure Modes & Trade-Offs: When to Avoid
sections.body: Improper implementation of REST API Design introduces operational bottlenecks and failure modes:
bullets: **Where to Avoid: Trade-Off Bottlenecks**: Avoid when constraints cannot tolerate: can cause over-fetching (returning 50 fields when mobile needs 3) or under-fetching (requiring multiple round-trips for nested graphs).

**Where to Avoid: Complexity Ceiling**: Avoid when operational requirements do not justify: breaks standard http url caching (all queries use `post /graphql`), vulnerable to expensive nested n+1 query dos without query depth limiters.
**Catastrophic Failure Modes**: Uncalibrated parameters can trigger queue exhaustion, thread starvation, cascading retry storms, and tail latency amplification.
**Operational Overhead**: Requires continuous observability (p95/p99 latency tracking, saturation alerts, and distributed tracing across hop boundaries).

subtopics.title: API Versioning
subtopics.subtitle: Evolving APIs safely without breaking existing mobile and third-party clients via URI paths, headers, and date-based pinned versions.
keyTakeaways: Once an API is consumed by external third parties or deployed mobile apps (where users don't update for months), breaking changes require explicit versioning.
Additive changes (adding new optional request fields or new response properties) are backward-compatible; renaming, removing, or changing field types is a breaking change.

URI Path Versioning (`/v1/orders`) is the most pragmatic and debuggable industry standard, while Stripe-style Date Header Pinning (`Stripe-Version: 2026-03-01`) excels for complex developer platforms.

sections.heading: 1. Architectural Fundamentals & Core Mechanics
sections.body: Every successful API eventually needs to change a data structure, for example, splitting a single `name: string` field into `first_name` and `last_name`, or changing a synchronous response into an asynchronous job. Because you cannot force every customer or iOS user on a 2-year-old app version to deploy simultaneously, you must support multiple contract versions concurrently during a deprecation window.
bullets: **Core Architectural Principle**: Once an API is consumed by external third parties or deployed mobile apps (where users don't update for months), breaking changes require explicit versioning.

**Problem Space & Invariants**: Additive changes (adding new optional request fields or new response properties) are backward-compatible; renaming, removing, or changing field types is a breaking change.
**System Boundary**: Operates across client network dispatch, gateway queuing, thread execution pools, and persistent storage I/O.

sections.heading: 2. Architectural Patterns & Implementation Topologies
sections.body: Distributed architectures apply specific implementation patterns and topologies for API Versioning:
bullets: **URI Path Versioning (/v1/resources, /v2/resources)**: Provides 100% explicit in curl, logs, documentation, and api gateway routing rules; impossible for a developer to miss which version they are calling. Best suited for 90% of public REST APIs, microservice endpoints, and mobile backend APIs.

**Header-Based Date Versioning (X-API-Version: 2026-03-01)**: Provides allows fine-grained, incremental breaking changes via composable request/response migration gates without changing urls. Best suited for Developer-first API platforms (Stripe, Twilio, GitHub) with hundreds of evolving endpoints and per-account version pinning.
1. URI Path Versioning (`/v1/users`, `/v2/users`): Explicit, visible in browser bars and server logs, trivial to route in any L7 Load Balancer or CDN.
2. Header / Media-Type Versioning (`Accept: application/vnd.company.v2+json` or `X-API-Version: 2026-03-01`): Keeps resource URLs pure and unchanging across versions.

Expand-and-Contract: First add the new field (`full_name`) alongside the old field (`name`), dual-populate both for 6 months while monitoring usage metrics, then remove the old field only when traffic hits 0%.
Sunset Headers: Return `Deprecation: true` and `Sunset: Wed, 11 Nov 2026 23:59:59 GMT` so client SDKs log automated warnings.

subtopics.title: Pagination
subtopics.subtitle: Why Offset/Limit pagination collapses on deep pages and real-time feeds, and how Keyset/Cursor pagination guarantees O(1) index performance.
keyTakeaways: Offset pagination (`LIMIT 20 OFFSET 100000`) forces the database to scan and discard 100,000 rows on disk (`O(N)` cost), causing severe latency spikes on deep pages.
Offset pagination also suffers from the **Page Drift (Duplicate/Skipped Row)** bug when new items are inserted at the top of a real-time feed while a user scrolls.
Cursor (Keyset) pagination encodes the last seen `(created_at, id)` tuple into an opaque token and uses an indexed `WHERE (created_at, id) < ($1, $2)` seek (`O(1)` cost).
subtopics.architectureDiagram:
OFFSET PAGINATION (O(N) Full Scan + Drift Bug!)
SELECT * FROM posts ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20 OFFSET 100000;
[DB Engine]: Scans 100,020 rows -> Discards first 100,000 -> Returns 20 (Slow!)

CURSOR / KEYSET PAGINATION (O(1) B-Tree Index Seek!)
SELECT * FROM posts WHERE (created_at, id) < ('2026-03-10T12:00Z', 'p_882')
ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 20;
[B-Tree Index]: Jumps directly to ('2026-03-10T12:00Z', 'p_882') -> Reads next 20!

sections.heading: 1. Architectural Fundamentals & Core Mechanics
sections.body: Beginner APIs implement pagination using `?page=5&limit=20`, which translates to `SELECT * FROM items ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20 OFFSET 80`. While this works for small admin tables, it fails catastrophically on large or rapidly mutating datasets for two reasons: (1) **Database I/O Amplification**: To serve `OFFSET 500,000`, PostgreSQL or MySQL must still walk through 500,000 index/heap entries just to count and throw them away. (2) **Data Drift on Inserts**: If a user loads Page 1 (items 1–20), and 3 new tweets arrive at the top before they request Page 2 (`OFFSET 20`), the user will see items 18, 19, and 20 duplicated at the top of Page 2!
bullets: **Core Architectural Principle**: Offset pagination (`LIMIT 20 OFFSET 100000`) forces the database to scan and discard 100,000 rows on disk (`O(N)` cost), causing severe latency spikes on deep pages.
**Problem Space & Invariants**: Offset pagination also suffers from the **Page Drift (Duplicate/Skipped Row)** bug when new items are inserted at the top of a real-time feed while a user scrolls.
**System Boundary**: Operates across client network dispatch, gateway queuing, thread execution pools, and persistent storage I/O.

sections.heading: 2. Architectural Patterns & Implementation Topologies
sections.body: Distributed architectures apply specific implementation patterns and topologies for Pagination:
bullets: **Cursor / Keyset Pagination (?cursor=eyJ.&limit=20)**: Provides constant o(1) database seek time whether on page 1 or page 100,000; immune to duplicate/skipped items during live inserts. Best suited for Infinite-scroll social feeds, chat message history, transaction logs, and high-scale public APIs.

**Offset / Limit Pagination (?page=3&limit=20)**: Provides supports numbered page buttons (`1, 2, 3 . 15`) in back-office data tables; trivial to combine with arbitrary ad-hoc column sorting. Best suited for Internal admin dashboards, small bounded datasets (< 10,000 rows), or search UIs capped at max 50 pages.
Deep Offset DoS Attack: Scrapers requesting `?page=50000` can easily bring down a production database with CPU-pegging offset scans.
COUNT(*) Overhead: Returning `total_pages: 48291` requires running `SELECT COUNT(*)` across millions of rows on every request.

Always Include a Unique Tie-Breaker: If 50 events occur in the same millisecond, `WHERE created_at < $1` will skip 49 of them! Always use a tuple comparison `WHERE (created_at, id) < ($1, $2)` backed by a composite index.
The `LIMIT + 1` Trick: Request `21` rows from the DB when the user asks for `limit=20`. If 21 rows return, slice off the 21st row and set `has_more: true`: zero extra queries needed!

**Where to Use: High-Throughput Scenarios**: Recommended for Internal admin dashboards, small bounded datasets (< 10,000 rows), or search UIs capped at max 50 pages, where Supports numbered page buttons (`1, 2, 3 . 15`) in back-office data tables; trivial to combine with arbitrary ad-hoc column sorting.

subtopics.title: Idempotency
subtopics.subtitle: Guaranteeing Exactly-Once side effects over At-Least-Once networks using Idempotency-Key headers, atomic locks, and cached responses.
keyTakeaways: In a distributed system, when a client experiences a network timeout on `POST /v1/payments`, it cannot know if the server crashed *before* or *after* charging the credit card.
Without idempotency, retrying a timed-out `POST` request causes catastrophic double-charges or duplicate orders.

True idempotency requires the client to generate a UUID `Idempotency-Key` per logical intent, and the server to atomically track key state (`IN_PROGRESS` vs `COMPLETED`) alongside the database mutation.
subtopics.architectureDiagram:
THE NETWORK TIMEOUT AMBIGUITY & IDEMPOTENCY KEY RESCUE
[ Client ]                                            [ Payment API + Redis/DB ]
    |--- 1. POST /pay (Idempotency-Key: "uuid-99") -------->|
    |                                                       |-- Lock Key "uuid-99"
    |                                                       |-- Charge Card ($50)
    |                                                       |-- Save Response (200 OK)
    |    X <--- (Network Drops Response Packet!) -----------|
    |
    |--- 2. RETRY POST /pay (Idempotency-Key: "uuid-99") -->|
    |                                                       |-- Key "uuid-99" Found!
    |<-- 3. Returns Cached 200 OK (Card NOT Charged Twice!)-|-- Skip Stripe Call

sections.heading: 1. Architectural Fundamentals & Core Mechanics
sections.body: An operation is **idempotent** if executing it multiple times produces the exact same system state and side effects as executing it once (`f(f(x)) = f(x)`). While `GET`, `PUT`, and `DELETE` are naturally idempotent by HTTP specification, `POST` (creating an order, transferring money, sending an email) is NOT. Because mobile networks drop packets and load balancers retry on `502/504`, distributed systems provide **At-Least-Once** message delivery over the wire. To achieve **Effectively-Once** business execution, the client generates a unique `Idempotency-Key: <UUIDv4>` header before the first attempt and reuses that exact same key across all retries of that operation.
bullets: **Core Architectural Principle**: In a distributed system, when a client experiences a network timeout on `POST /v1/payments`, it cannot know if the server crashed *before* or *after* charging the credit card.
**Problem Space & Invariants**: Without idempotency, retrying a timed-out `POST` request causes catastrophic double-charges or duplicate orders.
**System Boundary**: Operates across client network dispatch, gateway queuing, thread execution pools, and persistent storage I/O.

sections.heading: 2. Architectural Patterns & Implementation Topologies
sections.body: Distributed architectures apply specific implementation patterns and topologies for Idempotency:
bullets: **Redis-Backed Idempotency Cache (SET NX + TTL)**: Provides sub-millisecond lookup latency, automatic ttl expiration of old keys after 24h, offloads duplicate retry storms from hitting the primary sql db. Best suited for High-throughput API gateways, notification dispatchers, and general microservice POST endpoints.

**ACID Relational Table Idempotency (Same DB Transaction)**: Provides 100% atomic commit of both the business state change and the completed idempotency response; zero crash recovery window. Best suited for Payment gateways (Stripe/Adyen style), wallet transfers, order creation, and ledger accounting.

Payload Fingerprint Check: Store a SHA-256 hash of the request body alongside the `Idempotency-Key`. If a buggy client reuses the same key with different payment parameters, immediately return `422 Unprocessable Entity`.

Concurrent In-Flight Race Protection: If the client retries while Attempt #1 is still executing (`status === 'IN_PROGRESS'`), return `409 Conflict` (or wait on the lock) so two threads don't run simultaneously.
Database Unique Constraint Guard: `INSERT INTO payments (id, idempotency_key, amount) VALUES (.) ON CONFLICT (idempotency_key) DO NOTHING` makes double-insertion mathematically impossible.
Kafka / SQS Consumer Idempotency: Track processed `event_id`s in a deduplication table or use monotonic version checks (`WHERE version = $expectedVersion`) on target rows.

sections.body: Production deployments apply Idempotency across targeted operational scenarios:
bullets: **Where to Use: High-Impact Scenarios**: Optimal for High-throughput API gateways, notification dispatchers, and general microservice POST endpoints, suited for environments requiring Sub-millisecond lookup latency, automatic TTL expiration of old keys after 24h, offloads duplicate retry storms from hitting the primary SQL DB.

**Where to Use: High-Throughput Scenarios**: Recommended for Payment gateways (Stripe/Adyen style), wallet transfers, order creation, and ledger accounting, where 100% atomic commit of both the business state change and the completed idempotency response; zero crash recovery window.

**How to Use: Engineering Implementation**: Storing idempotency state in Redis and business state in PostgreSQL still leaves a tiny window where the process crashes after committing to PostgreSQL but before updating Redis. Always establish explicit thresholds, measurement baselines, and automated monitoring.

sections.heading: 2. Architectural Patterns & Implementation Topologies
sections.body: Distributed architectures apply specific implementation patterns and topologies for Rate Limiting:
bullets: **Token Bucket (2 fields in Redis Hash via Lua)**: Provides o(1) tiny memory footprint (16 bytes per user), naturally accommodates brief user bursts without false-positive 429s. Best suited for General user-facing REST/GraphQL APIs, SaaS tier quotas, and cloud control-plane APIs.

**Sliding Window Counter / Leaky Bucket**: Provides prevents boundary burst spikes (sliding window) or smooths outflow to a strict constant qps (leaky bucket) to protect fragile databases. Best suited for Protecting legacy third-party banking rails, SMS gateways, or strict per-second compliance limits.

1. Token Bucket (Stripe / AWS API Gateway): A bucket holds up to `B` tokens and refills at `R` tokens/sec. Each request consumes 1 token. Allows legitimate bursts up to `B` while capping long-term average rate to `R`. Memory footprint: just 2 numbers (`tokens`, `last_refill_ts`) per user!
2. Leaky Bucket (Shopify / Network Traffic Shaping): Requests enter a FIFO queue of fixed size and leak out at a strict constant rate. Smooths bursts completely, but adds queuing delay.
Standard Response Headers: `X-RateLimit-Limit: 100`, `X-RateLimit-Remaining: 42`, `X-RateLimit-Reset: 1710514800`, and `Retry-After: 15` on `HTTP 429`.

Fail-Open vs Fail-Closed: If the Redis rate-limiter cluster goes down, most user-facing APIs **fail open** (allow traffic through using local fallback memory limits) rather than taking down the entire company.

codeSnippet.title: Atomic Distributed Token Bucket in Redis Lua (Race-Condition Free)
codeSnippet.code:
-- Executed via EVALSHA on Redis so read + refill math + write runs atomically in <0.2ms!
-- KEYS[1] = "rl:bucket:user_123"
-- ARGV[1] = capacity (e.g. 20), ARGV[2] = refill_rate_per_ms, ARGV[3] = now_ms

local data = redis.call("HMGET", KEYS[1], "tokens", "last_ts")
local tokens = tonumber(data[1])
local last_ts = tonumber(data[2])
local capacity = tonumber(ARGV[1])
local rate = tonumber(ARGV[2])
local now = tonumber(ARGV[3])

if tokens == nil then
  tokens = capacity
  last_ts = now
else
  local elapsed = math.max(0, now - last_ts)
  tokens = math.min(capacity, tokens + (elapsed * rate))
  last_ts = now
end

if tokens >= 1 then
  tokens = tokens - 1
  redis.call("HMSET", KEYS[1], "tokens", tokens, "last_ts", last_ts)
  redis.call("EXPIRE", KEYS[1], 3600)
  return {1, math.floor(tokens)} -- Allowed (1) + remaining tokens
else
  return {0, 0}                  -- Rejected (429 Too Many Requests)
end

subtopics.title: API Gateway
subtopics.subtitle: Centralizing cross-cutting edge concerns: TLS termination, JWT validation, rate limiting, routing, and the Backend-for-Frontend (BFF) pattern.
keyTakeaways: An API Gateway is the single L7 entry point for external clients, offloading cross-cutting concerns (AuthN, Rate Limiting, WAF, TLS, Observability) from internal microservices.
The **Backend-for-Frontend (BFF)** pattern deploys tailored gateway layers per client type (Mobile BFF vs Web BFF vs Public API) to optimize payload shapes and aggregation.
Never put heavy business logic or synchronous cross-service orchestration loops inside a monolithic shared API Gateway, or it becomes an organizational bottleneck and SPOF.

bullets: **Single Centralized API Gateway (Kong / Envoy / AWS API GW)**: Provides uniform security, rate limiting, tls, and observability across the entire company; simple single domain (`api.company.com`) for clients. Best suited for Cross-cutting edge security, routing, rate limiting, and public developer APIs.

**Edge Gateway + Client-Specific BFFs (Mobile BFF, Web BFF)**: Provides frontend and mobile teams iterate autonomously on payload aggregation; reduces chatty mobile round-trips over cellular networks. Best suited for Organizations with distinct Web, iOS/Android, TV, and Public API experiences consuming a large microservice fleet.

1. Authentication Offload: Validates the client's JWT signature (using cached JWKS public keys) at the edge and forwards verified internal identity headers (`X-User-Id`, `X-Tenant-Id`) or an internal token to upstream services.
2. Rate Limiting & Quota Enforcement: Enforces per-tenant and per-IP token buckets before malicious traffic reaches internal compute.
Mobile BFF: Strips unnecessary fields, merges 4 internal gRPC calls via `Promise.allSettled()`, and formats payloads for mobile UI components.

Partial Failure Resilience: If the internal Recommendation Service times out during BFF aggregation, the BFF still returns 200 OK with the user's orders and an empty `recommendations: []` fallback array.

subtopics.title: Authentication / Authorization
subtopics.subtitle: Distinguishing AuthN (Who are you?) from AuthZ (What can you do?), Stateless JWTs vs Stateful Sessions, OAuth 2.0 / OIDC, and RBAC vs ABAC / ReBAC.
keyTakeaways: **Authentication (AuthN)** verifies identity (passwords, passkeys, OIDC, mTLS), whereas **Authorization (AuthZ)** enforces permissions (RBAC, ABAC, Google Zanzibar ReBAC).

Use a hybrid token strategy: short-lived (5–15 min) **Stateless JWT Access Tokens** verified locally via asymmetric public keys (RS256/EdDSA), paired with long-lived (7–30 day) **Stateful Refresh Tokens** that can be revoked in the database.

Never use symmetric `HS256` secrets across 50 microservices: if any one service leaks the secret, an attacker can forge admin tokens! Always use asymmetric `RS256` or `EdDSA` where only the Auth Service holds the Private Key and others verify with the Public Key (JWKS).

sections.heading: 1. Architectural Fundamentals & Core Mechanics
sections.body: Traditional web apps used **Stateful Session IDs**: on login, the server inserts a random ID into Redis/Postgres and returns `Set-Cookie: sid=xyz; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Strict`. Every subsequent API request requires a Redis lookup to resolve `sid -> user_id`, which makes instant revocation trivial (`DEL session:xyz`), but creates a central bottleneck at 500,000 QPS. **JSON Web Tokens (JWTs)** (`Header.Payload.Signature`) encode the user's ID, roles, and expiration (`exp`) directly into a cryptographically signed payload. Any microservice can verify a JWT's signature in `<0.1ms` CPU time using the Auth server's cached public key (`/.well-known/jwks.json`) with **zero database or network calls**.
bullets: **Core Architectural Principle**: **Authentication (AuthN)** verifies identity (passwords, passkeys, OIDC, mTLS), whereas **Authorization (AuthZ)** enforces permissions (RBAC, ABAC, Google Zanzibar ReBAC).

**Problem Space & Invariants**: Use a hybrid token strategy: short-lived (5–15 min) **Stateless JWT Access Tokens** verified locally via asymmetric public keys (RS256/EdDSA), paired with long-lived (7–30 day) **Stateful Refresh Tokens** that can be revoked in the database.
**System Boundary**: Operates across client network dispatch, gateway queuing, thread execution pools, and persistent storage I/O.

sections.heading: 2. Architectural Patterns & Implementation Topologies
sections.body: Distributed architectures apply specific implementation patterns and topologies for Authentication / Authorization:
bullets: **Short-Lived Stateless JWT (10m) + Stateful Refresh Token (30d)**: Provides zero database/network lookups on 99% of api calls, scales horizontally across global regions, supports immediate revocation on refresh or via tiny 10m blocklist. Best suited for Distributed microservice architectures, mobile apps, SPAs, and high-QPS global APIs.

**Opaque Stateful Session Cookies (Redis Lookup on Every Request)**: Provides instantaneous 0-second session revocation and permission updates, tiny cookie size, no cryptographic token payload exposed to client. Best suited for Monolithic web applications, banking portals requiring instant session kill-switches, and BFF-terminated browser sessions.

The JWT Revocation Problem: Because stateless JWTs aren't checked against a database, if a user is banned or logs out, their JWT remains valid until `exp`. Solution: Keep Access JWTs very short-lived (`5–15 minutes`) and pair them with a stateful, revocable **Refresh Token** (rotated on use).

Emergency Immediate Revocation: For critical security events (compromised account), broadcast only the revoked token's `jti` (or `user_id + revoked_at` timestamp) to a tiny Redis blocklist with a 15-minute TTL matching the Access Token's remaining lifespan.
RBAC (Role-Based Access Control): Users are assigned Roles (`Admin`, `BillingManager`), and Roles grant Permissions (`invoices:refund`). Simple and covers 80% of B2B SaaS needs.

ABAC (Attribute-Based Access Control): Evaluates dynamic attributes of the user, resource, and environment (e.g., 'Allow if `user.department == doc.department` AND `request.ip` is on corporate VPN', enforced via OPA / Cedar).
